sections.b: 2 Timothy is a letter in Paul's name to Timothy, written from prison in Rome when Paul expects to die. Chapter 1 urges Timothy not to be ashamed and to guard the deposit of teaching; chapter 2 tells him to entrust it to others, to endure like a soldier, athlete and farmer, and to correct false teachers gently; chapter 3 warns of the last days and points him to the God-breathed Scriptures; chapter 4 gives the last charge, Paul's farewell ("I have kept the faith") and his final requests.

Of the three Pastoral Letters, 2 Timothy is the most personal: it names more than twenty people, asks for a cloak and books (2 Timothy 4:13), and records desertions and a restored friendship with Mark (2 Timothy 4:10-11). It says almost nothing about church offices. These features have led some scholars to treat it apart from the other two. P. N. Harrison (1921) argued that a later Paulinist wrote all three but "had access to several brief personal notes written by the Apostle", which he added chiefly to 2 Timothy. 2 Timothy is sometimes said to be the most likely of the three to be Paul's, and Jerome Murphy-O'Connor was among those who defended its authenticity. C. F. D. Moule, as F. F. Bruce reports, suggested that Luke served as a secretary with unusual freedom. Many scholars on both sides read 2 Timothy as a farewell testament, a form often used for the last words of great figures. The travel notes (Trophimus left sick at Miletus, 2 Timothy 4:20) do not fit the journeys of Acts, which points either to a journey after Acts 28 or to a later writer.

2 Timothy shows Timothy through Paul's eyes at the end: his tears at their parting (2 Timothy 1:4), his faith learned from his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5), his knowledge of the holy writings from childhood (2 Timothy 3:15), the gift given when Paul laid hands on him (2 Timothy 1:6), and his witness of Paul's sufferings at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, the region of his home (2 Timothy 3:10-11). He is called to guard the teaching, entrust it to others, endure hardship and come to Rome before winter (2 Timothy 4:9, 21). Whether he reached Paul in time, the New Testament does not say.

2 Timothy presents Paul in chains in Rome, after a first hearing at which no one stood by him (2 Timothy 4:16), expecting death: "For I am already a drink offering being poured out, and the time for me to depart is here" (2 Timothy 4:6). Eusebius (Church History 2.22, 2.25) passes on what "is said": that Paul was released after Acts 28 and died on a second stay in Rome, where he wrote this letter, and he records that Paul was beheaded under Nero; 1 Clement 5 says he reached "the extreme limit of the west". Readers who think the letter was written after his death take it as the next generation's portrait of his last days.

common: 2 Timothy is Paul's last surviving letter, written shortly before his execution in Rome.
uncommon: 2 Timothy was written by a follower of Paul as a farewell testament, though it may preserve some of Paul's own notes.

sections.h: Paul in prison in Rome (2 Timothy)
sections.b: 2 Timothy is set in Rome, where Onesiphorus had to search hard to find the imprisoned Paul (2 Timothy 1:16-17), where Paul made his first defense (2 Timothy 4:16), and from where Eubulus, Pudens, Linus and Claudia send greetings (2 Timothy 4:21). Irenaeus later named Linus as the first bishop of Rome after the apostles (Against Heresies 3.3.3).

Tradition places Paul's last imprisonment and death under Nero: Eusebius says Paul was beheaded in Rome in Nero's persecution (Church History 2.25) and reads the "lion's mouth" of 2 Timothy 4:17 as Nero's cruelty (2.22). Tacitus describes Nero's punishment of the Christians after the fire of AD 64 (Annals 15.44).

2 Timothy seems to be sent to Timothy at or near Ephesus: Onesiphorus had served there (2 Timothy 1:18), Tychicus is being sent there (2 Timothy 4:12), and Prisca and Aquila and Onesiphorus' household are greeted (2 Timothy 4:19). "All those in Asia", the province of which Ephesus was the chief city, had turned away from Paul (2 Timothy 1:15).

Paul pictures his coming death as a drink offering already being poured out (2 Timothy 4:6), the end of a contest well fought and a race finished, with the crown of righteousness waiting (2 Timothy 4:7-8). The trustworthy saying of 2 Timothy 2:11-12 ("If we died with him, / we will live with him too") was heard by later martyrs as their own promise.

sections.h: Laying on of hands and handing on the teaching (2 Timothy)
sections.b: 2 Timothy 1:6 speaks of the gift in Timothy through the laying on of Paul's hands (1 Timothy 4:14 speaks of the elders' hands), and 2 Timothy 2:2 tells Timothy to entrust Paul's teaching to faithful people who will teach others. These verses are central to the churches' debate on ordination and apostolic succession; the card at 2 Timothy 2 sets out the Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and Reformed views.

Paul prays that Onesiphorus will "find mercy from the Lord on that day" and greets only his household (2 Timothy 1:16-18; 4:19). Some readers conclude that Onesiphorus had died, which would make this a prayer for the dead, and Catholic and Orthodox writers have cited it; others answer that he may only have been away from home. The card at 2 Timothy 1 gives the churches' views.

2 Timothy 1:18 ("May the Lord let him find mercy from the Lord on that day!") is one of the New Testament passages cited in the question of prayer for the dead, if Onesiphorus had died. See the topic "Purgatory and Prayers for the Dead" and the card at 2 Timothy 1.

sections.h: "If we deny him ... he stays faithful" (2 Timothy 2:12-13)
sections.b: The trustworthy saying of 2 Timothy 2:11-13 holds both sides of the question: "if we deny him, / he will deny us as well" is a warning, while "if we are unfaithful, / he stays faithful" is a promise. Readers who hold that true believers cannot finally fall away stress the promise; those who hold that they can, the warning; some distinguish passing unfaithfulness from final denial. The card at 2 Timothy 2 sets out the churches' answers.

sections.h: The deposit and the God-breathed Scriptures (2 Timothy)
sections.b: 2 Timothy joins two ideas that the churches weigh differently. Timothy must guard "the good deposit" and entrust what he heard from Paul to faithful people (2 Timothy 1:13-14; 2:2), and he must remain in the holy writings, for "Every Scripture is God-breathed and useful" (2 Timothy 3:14-17). Catholic and Orthodox teachers see both the handing on and the Scriptures as God's gift to the church; Protestant teachers see the apostolic deposit as now contained in Scripture, which is the rule for all teaching. The card at 2 Timothy 3 sets out the views.

"The holy writings" Timothy knew from childhood (2 Timothy 3:15) were the Jewish Scriptures, probably in the Greek Septuagint. Whether that collection already had fixed limits, and whether it included books such as Sirach and Wisdom, is part of the canon debate. 2 Timothy 3:16 is about the character of Scripture (God-breathed), not about its list of books.

sections.h: Hard times in the last days (2 Timothy 3)
sections.b: 2 Timothy 3:1-5 says that "in the last days hard times will set in" and lists the vices of people who keep the form of godliness without its power. Since Timothy is told to turn away from such people (2 Timothy 3:5), most readers take the last days as already present in the church's time; others read the list as a forecast of the end.

sections.h: Hymenaeus, Philetus and the teachers of 2 Timothy
sections.b: 2 Timothy names Hymenaeus and Philetus, who said "the resurrection has already taken place" (2 Timothy 2:17-18), compares opponents of the truth with Jannes and Jambres, Pharaoh's magicians (2 Timothy 3:8), and warns of a time when people will gather teachers to suit their desires and turn to myths (2 Timothy 4:3-4). The response it asks for is gentle correction in the hope of repentance (2 Timothy 2:24-26).

sections.h: "The resurrection has already taken place" (2 Timothy 2:18)
sections.b: Hymenaeus and Philetus taught that the resurrection was already past, most likely meaning a spiritual rising with no future bodily resurrection. 2 Timothy answers with "Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead" (2 Timothy 2:8), and with Christ who "has done away with death's power" and brought life and immortality to light (2 Timothy 1:10).

The Pastoral Letters call Christ's coming his "appearing" (epiphaneia). In 2 Timothy 1:10 it is his first coming; in 2 Timothy 4:1 and 4:8 his coming as Judge and King, and the crown is promised "to all who have set their love on his appearing" (2 Timothy 4:8).

sections.h: "Luke is the only one with me" (2 Timothy 4:11)
sections.b: In 2 Timothy Luke alone of Paul's traveling companions remains with him in prison in Rome (2 Timothy 4:11). Eusebius (Church History 2.22.6) noted that Luke was with Paul when this letter was written, and concluded that "it is probable that Luke wrote the Acts of the Apostles at that time", during Paul's first stay in Rome.
Paul, who once refused to take Mark with him (Acts 15:37-39), asks Timothy to bring Mark, "because he is of great use to me in the ministry" (2 Timothy 4:11), a sign that the break had healed.
2 Timothy 4:10 places Titus in Dalmatia, on the east coast of the Adriatic, apparently sent there on Paul's work.
"I have sent Tychicus to Ephesus" (2 Timothy 4:12): he may have carried the letter, or come to take Timothy's place so that Timothy could travel to Rome.
2 Timothy 4:19 greets "Prisca and Aquila", apparently back in or near Ephesus, with Prisca named first, as in Romans 16:3.

2 Timothy 2:19 quotes the Greek of Numbers 16:5, Moses' answer to Korah's revolt ("God knew those who are his"; 2 Timothy has "the Lord"), and applies it to the false teachers of its own day: God knows who belongs to him.

sections.h: Jannes, Jambres and the charlatans (2 Timothy 3)
sections.b: 2 Timothy compares the false teachers with Jannes and Jambres, the names Jewish tradition gave to Pharaoh's magicians (2 Timothy 3:8), and calls them goetes, "charlatans", a word that first meant sorcerers (2 Timothy 3:13). See the topic "Jannes and Jambres".
Paul calls his coming death a drink offering being poured out (2 Timothy 4:6): the wine poured out with Israel's sacrifices (Numbers 28:7), now a picture of a life given to God.

2 Timothy 3:16 is the only place in the Bible that uses the word theopneustos, "God-breathed". It says that Scripture comes from God and is useful for teaching, exposing wrong, putting things right and training in righteousness, so that "the man of God" is equipped. The Greek has no verb, so it can be read "every Scripture is God-breathed and useful" or "every God-breathed Scripture is also useful". The manuscripts do not differ in that clause. The Scripture Timothy knew was the Jewish Scriptures (2 Timothy 3:15).

2 Timothy 3:8-9 compares the false teachers with Jannes and Jambres, who "stood against Moses": like Pharaoh's magicians, they imitate the truth for a while, but their folly will be exposed, "just as the stupidity of those two became clear".
